readerTitle: Same work, same profit. Why one firm has cash and the other doesn't
caseNote: 가상 사례 (IT 지원 회사 두 곳, 욕실 리모델링 업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 제때 돈을 받는 일은 일이 끝난 뒤 독촉하는 문제가 아니라, 일을 시작하기 전에 정하는 결제 조건의 문제다.
misconception: 돈을 늦게 받는 건 고객이 늦게 내기 때문이고, 독촉을 잘하면 해결된다. 결제 조건을 까다롭게 말하면 고객을 잃는다.

sources.text: 재무관리의 표준 개념 (결제 조건, 매출채권 회수 기간 DSO, 2/10 net 30 조기 결제 할인)

factChecks.note: 훅 계산: 월 $40,000. 선청구·30일 결제 회사는 30일, 60일, 90일에 입금 → 90일까지 $120,000. 월말 청구·60일 결제 회사는 1개월 차 청구분이 90일에 첫 입금 → 90일까지 $40,000. 차이 $80,000.
신규 고객 계산: 월 $8,000, 월말 청구·net 60 → 첫 입금 약 90일째. 그때까지 제공한 일 3개월 = $24,000, 받은 돈 $8,000. 월초 선청구·net 30이면 30·60·90일에 입금되어 90일까지 $24,000.
조기 결제 할인 연이율: 2% 할인으로 20일 빨리 받음 → (2 ÷ 98) × (365 ÷ 20) ≈ 37.2%, 카드에는 "about 37% a year"로 표기.
욕실 공사: 계약 $12,000, 자재 $4,000을 첫 주에 구입. 일부 지역은 주택 공사 계약금 상한을 법으로 정합니다(예: 미국 일부 주). 카드에는 특정 법을 언급하지 않고 "check local rules"로만 적었습니다. 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Same work, same profit. Why one firm has cash and the other doesn't
body: Two IT support firms each bill $40,000 a month. Same clients, same costs, same profit.

The first bills at the start of each month, due in 30 days. The second bills at month-end, and clients pay in 60. By day 90, the first has collected **$120,000**. The second has collected $40,000 and is borrowing to make payroll.

image.label: Two identical offices, one with a full cash jar, one nearly empty
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 똑같이 생긴 작은 사무실 두 개가 나란히 있음. 왼쪽 사무실 앞 유리병에는 지폐가 가득, 오른쪽은 거의 비어 있음. 두 사무실 위에 같은 "$40,000 / month" 표지판. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: A big new client wants 60 days to pay.
body: You run a small IT support firm. A new client offers $8,000 a month, your biggest contract yet. Their standard terms: you invoice at month-end, they pay within 60 days. Your other clients pay within 30.

options.text: Accept their terms. Winning the deal matters most
options.feedback: You win the client, but you fund about three months of their support before the first payment arrives. Fine if you have the cash, painful if you don't.

options.text: Keep the price, but propose billing at the start of each month, due in 30 days
options.feedback: You give them the price they want and ask for timing instead. Many buyers can flex on timing more easily than on price.

options.text: Say no unless they pay a full year upfront
options.feedback: It protects your cash completely, but few large clients accept it. You may lose a good customer over a gap you could have narrowed.

cards.title: What 60 days really means.
body: Billed at the start of each month, due in 30 days, you'd have collected all **$24,000** by day 90. Same client, same price, a very different bank balance.

breakdown.detail: Invoiced at the end of each month

breakdown.detail: 30 days of work, then 60 days to pay

breakdown.label: Work delivered by then
breakdown.detail: Three months of support, wages already paid

cards.title: Payment terms set the gap
body: **Payment terms** are the agreed rules for when a customer pays: upfront, a deposit, on completion, or *net 30* (within 30 days of the invoice).

The time between doing the work and getting the cash is often called **days to collect** (accountants say *days sales outstanding*). Every day of that gap, you are lending your customer money, with no interest.

image.label: Timeline from work done to cash received, with the gap shaded
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Work starts", 가운데 "Invoice sent", 오른쪽 "Cash arrives". 일 시작부터 입금까지 구간을 빨간색으로 칠하고 "You're lending to your customer" 라벨.

cards.title: The gap is decided at three moments.
body: Most owners focus on chasing late payers. But the biggest lever comes earlier.
list: **Before the work:** deposits, billing in advance, payments at each stage
**At the invoice:** send it the day the work is done, with a clear due date and an easy way to pay
**After the due date:** a polite reminder schedule you follow every time, not when you remember
cards.callout: Most of the gap is set before the work starts.
cards.softwareNote: Subscription software billed yearly by card collects before delivering anything. The same company selling to large firms on net-60 invoices can look like the second IT firm.

cards.title: Faster isn't free.
body: Strict terms can cost you customers, especially large ones with the power to set their own. Push too hard and you may win the argument and lose the account.

Early-payment discounts look cheap but aren't. Giving 2% off to be paid 20 days sooner works out to about **37% a year**. That's worth it only when cash is truly tight. And chase politely: a reminder protects cash, a threat can end a relationship.

cards.title: Now it's a bathroom remodel.
body: You remodel bathrooms. A $12,000 job takes three weeks, and you buy $4,000 of tiles and fixtures in week one. Today, homeowners pay everything when the job is done.
How should you set terms for the next job?

options.text: Keep payment on completion. It's what customers like
options.feedback: Customers are happy, but you carry $4,000 of materials and three weeks of wages. One slow payer and you're short for the next job.

options.text: Ask for the full $12,000 before you start
options.feedback: Your cash is safe, but many homeowners won't hand over everything before seeing any work. You trade trust for safety.

options.text: A deposit to cover materials, a payment midway, the balance on completion
options.feedback: Each payment roughly matches what you've spent, and the customer pays as they see progress. Check local rules, as some places limit deposits.

cards.title: Decide when you get paid before you start the work.
body: The gap between work and cash is a choice you make at the deal, not a fate you suffer after the invoice.
**Try it today:** list your five biggest customers. For each, count the days from finishing the work to cash in the bank. Pick one where you could ask for a deposit or earlier billing.
